source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Prompting or telling learners to self-explain beats not doing so, with a medium effect.
numbers: Random effects, 69 effect sizes, 64 reports, N=5917. g=.552, 95% CI .454-.650. Q=196.63 (df 68), I2=65.4%.
limits: Heterogeneity is large. Mostly undergraduates; many studies did not report time on task.
agent_relevance: Gives a prior of about g=0.5 for a one-line self-explanation step. Expect real but moderate gains.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Effect depends on the comparison. Largest versus nothing extra; smaller versus a given instructional explanation, but still positive.
numbers: No additional explanation g=.673 (k=41, N=3141); mixed g=.462 (k=15); instructional explanation g=.354 (k=6, N=573); other strategy g=.304 (k=7, N=516). QB=11.65, p=.009.
quote: Contrary to the coverage hypothesis ... our results showed a statistically detectable advantage (g = .35) of self-explanation over instructional explanations
limits: Only 6 studies in the instructional-explanation arm.
agent_relevance: An agent that writes its own explanation may do better than one handed a ready explanation, but a plain baseline gives the biggest gap.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: How the prompt is worded or timed mostly did not matter. Format cells are tiny.
numbers: Timing: concurrent g=.521 (k=57), retrospective g=.571 (k=8), beginning g=1.241 (k=4). Format: interrogative g=.559 (k=36), imperative g=.395 (k=12), predirected g=.700 (k=8), fill-in-blank g=.895 (k=2), multiple choice g=.242 not significant (k=2).
limits: Multiple-choice (k=2) and beginning (k=4) cells are tiny. Authors say variation in prompt features rarely mattered.
agent_relevance: A short free-form explanation line is fine. Do not turn it into a menu.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Type of explanation changed results: conceptual and anticipatory helped; metacognitive (plan or performance) prompts did not.
numbers: Conceptualize g=.873 (k=13); metacognitive g=.192 ns (k=3, N=241). Anticipatory g=1.37 (one study) vs justify own decisions g=.42, justify another person g=.43.
limits: Anticipatory estimate rests on one study.
agent_relevance: The target is content (why this step is valid), not 'how am I doing?'.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Benefit held across knowledge types and outcome types.
numbers: Conceptual g=.598 (k=33); procedural g=.468 (k=3); knowledge type QB=.861, p=.65. Problem solving g=.445 (k=14); transfer g=.534 (k=17); inference g=1.794 (k=2). Essay-question outcomes g=.624 ns (CI -.185 to 1.433, k=3).
limits: Few procedural studies.
agent_relevance: Supports use for step checking and for transfer-style questions.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Age holds from elementary to undergraduate; East Asia studies are an outlier.
numbers: Elementary g=.483 (k=10); high school g=.426 (k=13); undergraduate g=.611 (k=42). North America g=.525 (k=42); Europe g=.481 (k=18); East Asia g=1.191 (k=6).
limits: Authors tie East Asia to text-study tasks with no-explanation controls; confound, not culture proven.
agent_relevance: No sign the effect needs high expertise. Do not read culture effects from this data.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Time on task is the main threat. Self-explanation usually costs more time and few studies controlled it. Publication bias tests do not threaten the result.
numbers: More-time studies g=.72 vs similar-time g=.41, difference not significant. Fail-safe N 6028 (Rosenthal); Orwin: 274 missing null studies to fall under 0.1.
quote: most research on self-explanation has, regrettably, not fully reported time-on-task
limits: Efficiency may be exaggerated because time was often unreported.
agent_relevance: Count tokens spent. Even g=.41 at similar time is positive.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Studies that verified treatment fidelity gave somewhat different effects (not significant).
numbers: Fidelity analyzed g=.613 (k=31); no check g=.409 (k=21); followed-up g=.587 (k=11); not reported g=.732 (k=6). QB=4.74, p=.19.
limits: Not significant.
agent_relevance: Check that the model really wrote an explanation, not a token one.

source: McEldoon, Durkin & Rittle-Johnson (2013) Is self-explanation worth the time? (as described by Bisra 2018 and Chen 2026)
finding: Time-matched test in elementary maths: self-explanation versus extra practice problems. Little difference across problem types and outcomes.
numbers: Bisra: little difference between time-matched self-explanation and additional-problem conditions. Chen et al. say the advantage disappeared. Exact N not read.
limits: Secondhand; original paywalled. Used unprompted verbal explanations with no feedback on quality.
agent_relevance: Boundary: with equal budget spent on extra attempts the gain can vanish. Test the S5 line against more samples at equal tokens.

source: Chi, de Leeuw, Chiu & LaVancher (1994) Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding (as described by Bisra 2018)
finding: Founding prompted experiment: 8th graders on circulatory system text. Prompted self-explainers beat rereaders but studied almost twice as long.
numbers: About 1 hour longer study; they could return for another session, so spacing may add to the effect (Bisra reading). No scores read.
limits: Secondhand; original blocked.
agent_relevance: The classic result is confounded with time.

source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann & Glaser (1989) Self-explanations (as described by Bisra 2018)
finding: Founding observational study: students differ stably in how much they explain examples, and this tracks learning.
numbers: No numbers read. Bisra: self-explanation could be an effect rather than a cause of learning. Renkl (1997): successful learners predicted the next step or explained goal structure.
limits: Correlational; secondhand.
agent_relevance: 1989 shows who self-explains, not that prompting helps; the 2018 meta-analysis gives the causal evidence.

source: Schworm & Renkl (2006) and Renkl (2002) (as described by Bisra 2018)
finding: Offering an instructional explanation on request after self-explanation prompts did not help; prompts alone did better.
numbers: Prompts-only group outperformed prompts plus on-demand explanation (no figures in Bisra).
limits: Secondhand. Renkl 2002 proposal (explain first, supply on request) was not supported.
agent_relevance: If the agent sees a reference answer, showing it too early may reduce its own effort. Explain first, then check.

source: Lawson & Mayer (2021) Benefits of writing an explanation during pauses in multimedia lessons
finding: Three experiments, college students, 4-part online greenhouse-gas lesson. Writing an explanation after each part helped on a delayed test but not an immediate one.
numbers: Exp 1: no differences on immediate posttest. Exp 2 delayed: write-an-explanation M=8.06 (SD 4.02) vs no-activity M=5.41 (SD 3.78), p=.018; focused explanation M=7.27, p=.167 ns; read-an-explanation M=4.47, p=.729 ns. Write > read p=.001. F(3,127)=6.83.
limits: Writing groups took about 3x longer (9m42s and 10m10s vs 3m15s and 3m05s). Within-group time did not predict score (r=.05 to .12) but time is not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Test on later steps, not only the immediate answer. Reading a given explanation did nothing.

source: Lawson & Mayer (2021), citing Fiorella & Mayer (2015)
finding: Prompted explaining beat controls in most tests.
numbers: 44 of 54 experimental tests favored explaining; median d=0.61.
limits: Secondhand figure from the intro; text and multimedia lessons.
agent_relevance: A second estimate close to Bisra g=.55.

source: Lawson & Mayer (2021) Experiment 3 abstract
finding: Rewriting a given explanation also helped on a delayed test.
numbers: Abstract: write (Exp 2, 3), focused write (Exp 2) and rewrite (Exp 3) groups beat no-activity on delayed posttest. Exp 3 numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Re-expressing content may be enough; producing text matters more than novelty.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More: LLM-Supported Self-Explanation in Calculus
finding: Between-subjects test of LLM feedback on written self-explanations under fixed 60-minute practice. No gain on ordinary post-test; gain only in LLM-scored explanation quality on one transfer type.
numbers: N=92 (control 29, menu 35, open-ended 28). NEI transfer explanation +11.9 points, p=.030, d=0.44, CI [1.2, 22.6]. Combined explanations +7.3, p=.057, d=0.38. NEI multiple choice +9.3, p=.183 ns. Gains: control +9.4, menu +5.9, open-ended +9.3. Problems done: 58.9 vs 43.8 vs 16.9.
limits: Small N; 105 failed screening and 104 dropped out. Many outcomes tested, one below .05. Graded by GPT-5.1 (kappa .78 with human consensus, .66-.68 with single graders). Menu gave no gain.
agent_relevance: With equal time, explanation plus LLM feedback matched learning with a third of the problems. Free text beat menu. Gain is in explaining, not answer accuracy.

source: Chen et al. (2026) Practice Less, Explain More
finding: Authors argue earlier time-matched failures (Matthews & Rittle-Johnson; McEldoon) used unprompted verbal explanations without feedback on quality, unlike their LLM-feedback condition.
numbers: Cites those two as the time-matched failures.
limits: Authors interpretation; their design cannot separate feedback from explanation.
agent_relevance: The explanation step may need a quality check (a verifier), not just a request.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan et al. (2026) Self-Explanation Tutor for Active Study of CS1 Worked Examples (ESSE)
finding: LLM as judge of student self-explanations of code lines: reliable on correctness against experts and crowd, weaker on completeness.
numbers: 358 expert-rated attempts: precision .95, recall .87, F1 .91, accuracy 83.8%, kappa .32 (skewed labels); 42 false negatives vs 16 false positives. Crowd (124 workers, 1,696 ratings, 216 explanations): precision .90, recall .95, F1 .93. Completeness AUC .67 vs expert. Revised 63% after an incorrect verdict, 35% after a correct one.
limits: 8 students; only 3 completed the posttest (gains .67, -.25, .78). No control group.
agent_relevance: An LLM can judge a step explanation with F1 about .9 but under-credits correct ones. Use it as a flag.

source: Lekshmi-Narayanan et al. (2026) ESSE
finding: Feedback made students add concepts, not just words.
numbers: Completeness vs change in word count rho=-.49; mixed model concept coefficient .50 vs volume .33. 38% of explanations got a second attempt (83 of 216); 37% of those a third (31 of 83). 5 of 8 said feedback helped them write more.
limits: Self-report, tiny N.
agent_relevance: Short verdicts (wrong / incomplete) drove useful revision, as in a one-line S5 note.

source: Gao et al. (2023) Self-Explanation Prompting Improves Dialogue Understanding in LLMs
finding: Zero-shot prompt to explain each dialogue utterance before answering beat chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve on 6 dialogue sets (gpt-3.5-turbo).
numbers: MultiWOZ 2.1 JGA: vanilla 35.93, CoT 27.64, plan-and-solve 39.19, 4-shot 41.60, self-explanation 44.44, with GPT-4 50.97. STARv2: 51.88 / 51.85 / 56.74 / 52.93 / 63.66 / GPT-4 70.27. MuTual GPT-4 91.87. MELD only 59.14 to 61.71.
limits: Not the human sense: utterance-by-utterance analysis, not explaining a worked example. Single run, no variance.
agent_relevance: Explain each unit before using it can beat generic step-by-step. CoT hurt MultiWOZ, so explanations are not automatically good.

source: Gao et al. (2023) trigger-sentence ablation
finding: Wording matters: vague understand-first barely helps; explain-every-utterance helps most.
numbers: MultiWOZ JGA: vanilla 35.93; understand 36.52; summarize 40.98; explain by utterance 44.44.
limits: One dataset and model.
agent_relevance: A specific explain-each-unit instruction beats a vague one.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) Can language models learn from explanations in context?
finding: Adding explanations to few-shot examples helps large LMs; matched control explanations do not, so the example-explanation link matters.
numbers: 40 tasks, models 1B to 280B parameters, hierarchical regression. Untuned explanations help; explanations hand-tuned on a small validation set and joint selection of examples plus explanations help more. Smaller models do not benefit.
limits: Explanations were human-written, not self-generated. Effect sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: Explanation helps only when the model is large enough, like the prior-knowledge limit in people.

source: Ye & Durrett (2022) The Unreliability of Explanations in Few-shot Prompting for Textual Reasoning
finding: Weak result: explanations in the prompt give small gains for most LLMs, and generated explanations are often not factual or not entailing.
numbers: InstructGPT: SYNTH 54.8 to 58.5, ADVHOTPOT 56.8 to 59.4; E-SNLI order effects mixed (+2.6 for one order, other lagged). text-davinci-002 gained more. A factuality check on explanations lifted SYNTH accuracy from 52.4% to 74.8%.
limits: 2022 models, two NLP tasks, order effect task-specific.
agent_relevance: Do not treat the model own explanation as proof. Check it against the input.

source: Zelikman et al. (2022) STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
finding: Training analogue: given the right answer as a hint, the model writes a rationale (rationalization); rationales are kept when they reach correct answers.
numbers: CommonsenseQA dev: 68.8 without rationalization, 72.5 with (GPT-J), vs 73.0 for a fine-tuned model 30x larger; +35.9% over few-shot. GSM8K: few-shot CoT 3.1, direct finetune 5.8, STaR 10.1, with rationalization 10.7.
limits: Fine-tuning, not a scaffold. Needs known-correct answers.
agent_relevance: Explaining a known-correct step works like a worked example. Outcome filtering needs a checker.

source: Mahzari group (2018) Teaching clinical reasoning through hypothetico-deduction is (slightly) better than self-explanation
finding: Rival method beat self-explanation: hypothesizing several diagnoses beat explaining the case, one week later.
numbers: N=88 second-year medical students, small groups, 7 vignettes. Accuracy hypothetico-deduction M=0.22 (SD .14) vs self-explanation M=0.17 (SD .12); F(1,88)=4.90, p=.03, partial eta2=.06.
limits: One session; low absolute scores; small effect. Authors suggest benefit came from forming more than one hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Self-explanation is not always best; generating multiple hypotheses can beat explaining one. Pair the S5 line with alternatives.

source: Feedback after self-explanation in diagnostic reasoning, Canadian medical school study (2019)
finding: Adding the correct diagnosis as feedback after self-explanation helped near transfer but not far transfer.
numbers: N=94 third-year students, 3 conditions. Near-transfer accuracy: immediate feedback M=90.73 (SD 10.69), delayed M=89.92 (SD 13.85), control M=82.03 (SD 17.66), p<.05. Far transfer: no difference.
limits: Feedback was the final answer only, one-week delay.
agent_relevance: Naming the right answer fixes similar cases only. For far transfer say what principle was wrong.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Rival accounts: coverage (adds missing information) vs generation (own links to prior knowledge). Meta-analysis favours generation in part.
numbers: g=.35 over scripted explanation (k=6); g=.67 over no explanation (k=41).
limits: The discriminating test has only 6 studies; coverage may explain about half.
agent_relevance: A verifier supplies coverage; the model own writing supplies generation.

source: Bisra et al. (2018) Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis
finding: Prompted explanations may fit knowledge gaps less well than spontaneous ones; observational links cannot show prompts help.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: Argument, not data.
agent_relevance: Trigger explanation where confidence is low, not on every step.
